description: A large fridge egg needs 4 minutes 30 seconds for a soft-boiled egg with a runny yolk. Times by size, start, and altitude, from the Williams formula.

examples.result: Two medium fridge eggs, soft-boiled: 4 minutes 10 seconds.
steps: A medium egg weighs 50 grams (USDA size).
The eggs start at fridge temperature, 4°C, and the water boils at 100°C at sea level.
The soft target is 63°C at the edge of the yolk.
The formula gives 249 seconds, about 4 minutes 10 seconds.

faqs.answer: A large fridge egg takes 4 minutes 30 seconds in boiling water. A medium egg takes 4 minutes 10 seconds and a jumbo 5 minutes 15 seconds. Start the timer when the egg goes into water that is already boiling.
faqs.question: How long does a soft-boiled egg take from the fridge?

faqs.answer: The formula times the edge of the yolk reaching 63°C, and the center lags behind. That cool, runny center is what a soft-boiled egg is. If you want the yolk warm all the way through, test kitchens land longer: Food Network Kitchen found 6 to 7 minutes for a runny large fridge egg.
faqs.question: Why is the yolk still cool in the middle?

faqs.answer: A minute in cold water is enough. It stops the carryover cooking that would turn a runny yolk jammy, and it cools the shell so you can hold the egg. A full ice bath is for hard-boiled eggs you plan to peel.
faqs.question: Does a soft-boiled egg need an ice bath?

faqs.answer: Yes, and they need less time: a large room-temperature egg takes 3 minutes 20 seconds. Room-temperature eggs also crack less often, because the shell does not get the same sudden shock.
faqs.question: Can I soft-boil eggs from room temperature?

faqs.answer: The edge of the yolk reaches about 63°C (145°F) when the white is set and the yolk still runs. The yolk starts to thicken between 65°C and 70°C, so a soft-boiled egg stops just short of that range.
faqs.question: What temperature is a soft-boiled yolk?

felicityNote: The dippy egg is my kids' favorite breakfast, and the timer is the whole secret. Four and a half minutes, cold water, toast soldiers, done.

parts.meaning: The constant from the egg's thermal properties: density 1.038 g per cubic cm, specific heat 3.7, thermal conductivity 0.0054.
The weight of the egg in grams. A large egg is 57 g (USDA size).
The starting temperature of the egg: 4°C from the fridge, 20°C at room temperature.
The boiling point of the water: 100°C at sea level, lower at altitude.
The target temperature at the edge of the yolk: 63°C for soft-boiled.
The yolk edge factor. The yolk is about a third of the egg, so its edge sits about 69 percent of the way from the center to the shell.

formula.text: Time = 27 × M^(2/3) × ln(0.76 × (Tegg - Twater) / (Tyolk - Twater)). For a large fridge egg at sea level, soft-boiled: 27 × 57^(2/3) × ln(0.76 × (4 - 100) / (63 - 100)) = 272 seconds, about 4 minutes 30 seconds.

howToSteps.name: Boil the water first
howToSteps.text: Fill a saucepan with enough water to cover the eggs by an inch and bring it to a full rolling boil. The formula assumes the egg goes into water that is already boiling.

howToSteps.name: Lower the eggs in
howToSteps.text: Lower each egg in gently on a spoon and start the timer the moment the first egg touches the water. Keep the water at a gentle boil.

howToSteps.name: Time it
howToSteps.text: Boil a large fridge egg for 4 minutes 30 seconds. A medium egg needs 4 minutes 10 seconds, an extra-large 4 minutes 55 seconds, and a jumbo 5 minutes 15 seconds.

howToSteps.name: Cool it fast
howToSteps.text: Lift the egg out with a slotted spoon and put it straight into cold water for a minute. This stops the cooking and keeps the yolk runny.

howToSteps.name: Serve it at once
howToSteps.text: Tap the top, peel it back, and eat the egg from the shell with toast soldiers, or peel it carefully and set it on toast.

title: How Long to Boil Soft-Boiled Eggs
tutorial: A soft-boiled egg is a white that holds its shape around a yolk that still runs. The formula times the moment the edge of the yolk reaches 63°C, which is where the yolk just starts to thicken. The white is already set by then, because the white sits against the shell and heats first. For a large fridge egg that moment comes at 4 minutes 30 seconds.

Size moves the time more than most people expect. A medium egg at 50 grams needs 4 minutes 10 seconds, and a jumbo at 71 grams needs 5 minutes 15 seconds. That is a minute of difference across the carton, and it is why the size on the box matters more than the brand. The time grows with the weight to the power of two thirds, so doubling the weight would not double the time.

Starting temperature matters too. The same large egg at room temperature needs 3 minutes 20 seconds, more than a minute less than from the fridge. If your eggs sit on the counter, use the room temperature setting. If they come straight from the fridge, keep the fridge setting and lower them in gently on a spoon, because a cold egg in boiling water is the one that cracks.

One honest note: the formula times the yolk edge, not the whole yolk. At 4 minutes 30 seconds the center of the yolk is still cool, which is exactly right for a dippy egg with toast soldiers. If you want the yolk warm right through, test kitchens that time the whole egg land longer: Food Network Kitchen found 6 to 7 minutes for a runny large fridge egg. The calculator gives you the physics answer; your spoon tells you the rest.

Whatever time you use, move the egg to cold water the moment the timer ends. The heat already in the white keeps travelling inward, and a soft yolk turns jammy in a minute or two on the counter. A bowl of cold water stops that carryover cooking and makes the shell easier to peel.
